title: Bo: darkness that could be felt (Exodus 10:21–23)
hookLine: three days so dark "they saw not one another"; yet in Israel's homes there was light

cards: During a power cut at night, the first thing most people do isn't look for a flashlight. It's call out. Are you okay?
Where are you? Darkness doesn't only hide the furniture. It hides the people.

The ninth plague is darkness, and the Torah describes it less like night and more like a weight. It came after the locusts, it lasted three days, and the most striking line about it isn't about the sky at all.
It's about what people could no longer see in each other.

teach.b: Moses stretches out his hand toward heaven, and a thick darkness covers Egypt. The old Jewish translation calls it "darkness which may be felt." Darkness you could touch.
For three days, "they saw not one another, neither rose any from his place." Not just the road. They couldn't see each other, and because of that, nobody got up.
A teaching often told in Hasidic circles reads those two halves as cause and effect. The darkest darkness, it says, is when a person doesn't see his brother.
Stop seeing the person next to you, and you can't move. You stay stuck in your place.
The verse ends with a turn: "but all the children of Israel had light in their dwellings." The Torah doesn't explain how. Commentators offered many answers; the plain text stays quiet.
But notice where the light was: in homes, among people. The midrash also wonders why the darkness lasted three days, and gives several reasons, none of them in the verse itself.
What the verse gives is the picture: one land where nobody could see anybody, and homes where people could. A dark time can be a whole country's or one person's.
Grief does it. Depression does it. A long illness, a lost job.
The person inside often can't rise from their place. Someone else, with light, can see them.

how: The ten plagues are recited at the Passover seder, a drop of wine spilled for each, and darkness is the ninth. Jewish tradition counts visiting and checking on people who are ill or grieving, bikur cholim and comforting mourners, as a mitzvah.

games.q: three days of darkness you can feel. what does the verse say happened to the Egyptians?
o: they lit fires and carried on.

they fled to Israel's homes for light.
games.why: nobody could see anybody, and nobody moved. a Hasidic teaching reads it: when you don't see your brother, you can't rise.

practice: Let a few faces come to mind and ask who's had the lights go out lately: a friend who's gone quiet, a neighbor after a loss, a relative who's stopped answering.
Let one face stay, and without fixing anything, just see them properly, the way you'd call out in a power cut. If you pray, you can hold them there for a while.

wordCard.voice: Bo. Still our portion. Today its ninth plague: darkness so thick no one could see another person, and light in Israel's homes.

orig.note: Hebrew: darkness. the same word as the darkness over the deep in Genesis 1.

carryVoice: Your line: see your brother. Brother, sister, friend, stranger: whoever is sitting in the dark. See you tomorrow.
